title: Words in Context, Part 2: A Hard Question and Common Traps

beats.say: In part one, we learned to cover the choices, find the clue, and put our own word in the blank first.
We saw that contrast words flip the meaning, and that a restatement defines the blank.
In this video, we work through a hard question with a distracting last sentence, and then the common traps.
beats.item: Today: a hard question and traps

beats.say: Hard question. Two choices may point in the right direction, and only one fits the exact degree and tone. Also ask who is being described.
Some texts add a last sentence about a different group of people. That sentence can distract you from the group that the blank describes.

scenes.title: Read the text
scenes.text: Early reviewers dismissed the composer's first symphony as ______, noting that nearly every melody seemed borrowed from works by more established composers. Only decades later did critics recognize the inventive ways she had rearranged those familiar themes.

beats.say: The clue follows the comma. Nearly every melody seemed borrowed. Our own word for that's copied.
The verb dismissed tells us the tone is negative. So the blank is a negative word about copying.
The last sentence describes critics decades later, not the early reviewers. That's the distraction, so we don't use it.

scenes.title: Which word fits the blank?
scenes.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

beats.say: Choice A, chaotic, means disorderly. Borrowing melodies isn't the same as disorder, so it doesn't fit the clue.
Choice C, incomplete, means unfinished. Nothing in the text says the symphony was unfinished.
Choice D, ambitious, is a positive word. But the reviewers dismissed the work, which is a negative judgment, so the tone is wrong.
Choice B, imitative, means copying others. It fits the borrowed melodies and the negative tone. The answer is B.
Now the traps. Each one is a way that a careful reader can still pick a wrong answer. We'll see the trap, and then the habit that avoids it.
Trap one. Students pick the hardest word because it sounds impressive. Hard vocabulary isn't automatically right.
beats.wrong_why: Sounding smart is not a clue

beats.say: Pick the word that matches your own prediction. Many correct answers are simple words.
beats.right: pick the word that fits the clue

beats.say: Trap two. If the text says a change was small, a word like devastating points in the right direction but is far too strong.
Match the degree as well as the direction. A small change calls for a mild word.
Trap three. In a sentence like critics said one thing, but later scholars found another, the blank describes only one group.
beats.wrong_why: The blank is about the early view

beats.say: Find the people the blank describes, and use only the clue about them.
Trap four. If the sentence is disapproving, a positive word can't fit, even if its meaning is close to the topic.
Check whether each word is positive or negative, and match it to the tone of the sentence.
Trap five. Two words can both relate to the topic, but only one fits the sentence structure. Withstand and resist both go with strong winds.
beats.wrong: the tower will resist the wind

beats.say: Test each word in the sentence and ask if the full meaning is right. Read it back as a whole.
To recap. Predict your own word, and check the direction, the degree, and the tone of every choice.
Find the group the blank describes, and ignore distracting sentences about other people.
In the next topic, we study text structure and purpose, where you say what a text is doing.
